video_title: Building AI Tools for the Military | Bharat Patel
gist: Bharat Patel, a former Army acquisition PM (Project Maven, Project Linchpin/AI Ops, TITAN) now leading AI and data for Accenture's defense portfolio, argues the binding constraint on military AI is not models but the 'boring' data pipeline: continuous operational data collection, labeling, T&E, and modular, rapid model redeployment. He says the US lacks Ukraine-style continuous data collection, synthetic data cannot substitute for real representative data, acquisition reform (PAEs) is still sorting out authorities, and the Pentagon's current product fascination will give way to demand for large integrators.

themes.theme: Data pipeline as the real bottleneck

insights.claim: Patel argues data will never be 'AI ready' in the abstract; the specific AI use case should determine what data and what quality level is needed, and organizations often focus on the wrong problem by cleaning data before choosing use cases.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Defense data-readiness contracts sold generically are less valuable than use-case-driven data work; favor vendors tying data engineering to specific missions.
insights.quote: In my opinion, data will never be AI ready. Data will always have its uh weirdness about it.

insights.claim: In the early phase of Project Maven (started 2016), much of the incoming data lacked the relevant targets, so computer vision models underperformed once operational, forcing the team to adopt continuous collection of relevant data.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Operational CV performance depends on recurring relevant-data collection, implying sustained (not one-off) spend on collection and labeling.

insights.claim: For an Army Research Lab tank model using second-gen FLIR imagery, no usable tank data existed, so the team had to build a physical data-collection box next to the sensor to capture enough data to train on.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Edge data capture hardware and sensor instrumentation are a prerequisite market for military AI, not an afterthought.

insights.claim: Patel expects an explosion of multimodal sensor data because autonomy will only be achieved by fusing multiple sensors rather than relying on a single sensor like imagery.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Watch sensor-fusion, multimodal data management and edge storage vendors as defense autonomy scales.

insights.claim: Patel says the department has no active data collection strategies for continuous machine learning; exercise data is usually erased, deleted, or dumped into storage where it loses context because storing and using it is resource intensive.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: A large unaddressed gap in DoD data custody/retention suggests future program spend on data infrastructure and governance.
insights.quote: There's no active data collection strategies for machine learning for continuous machine learning.

insights.claim: Ukraine's current autonomy capabilities stem from a long period of deliberate data collection from human-piloted drone video and sensors, which was later fed back to build target identification and more autonomous platforms.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Battlefield data accumulation is a compounding moat; the US lags absent a war or a deliberate collection program.
insights.quote: So what you see today in Ukraine is not how it started.

insights.claim: Patel says the 'boring side of AI' (data collection processes, standards, governance, infrastructure) is starting to get more attention, citing CDAO's scaffolding initiative as a positive sign.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: CDAO scaffolding-type initiatives are a signal of where DoD AI infrastructure dollars may flow.
insights.quote: I 100% believe that um the boring side of AI is is now starting to become more popular.

insights.claim: Rather than building reliable models from military exercises, which may not represent the next fight, Patel says the priority should be the speed of the full pipeline: collect data, bring it back, train, test and evaluate, and push models back out.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Rapid retrain-and-redeploy pipeline capability (MLOps for defense) is the key procurement category to track.
insights.quote: the way that we do our exercises may not be representative of what the next fight looks like

themes.theme: Government vs. industry division of labor

insights.claim: Patel's ideal setup is that the government owns and manages the data and the pipeline governance, but industry does roughly 90% of the work across data management, labeling, T&E, deployment and model training.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Defense AI spend should be broad across many pipeline sub-segments, favoring contractors in labeling, T&E and deployment.
insights.quote: But industry should be doing like 90% of the work.

insights.claim: Patel says the government should break the AI pipeline into modular pieces so it can iterate continuously with industry and never be locked into a single industry partner longer than needed.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Modular procurement design caps incumbency advantages; single-vendor platform plays face recompete risk.

insights.claim: Project Linchpin, now Product Manager AI Ops and Services, was originally structured to allow maximum industry participation in the AI pipeline.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
entities: Product Manager AI Ops and Services
insights.so_what: Army AI Ops program is designed as a multi-vendor marketplace, an entry point for smaller AI firms.

insights.claim: Patel views the new Portfolio Acquisition Executives (PAEs) as another attempt to accelerate acquisition that does not tackle the hard part: holding the authorized program manager accountable and giving them adequate resources.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Do not assume PAE restructuring will quickly accelerate contract awards; expect lingering friction.

insights.claim: For the past few months there has been confusion over what must be authorized at the PAE level versus CPEs, PMs and product managers; in theory PAEs' greater pull over requirements and contracting should speed requirement changes once settled.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Near-term award timing may slip during the reorg, with potential acceleration later.
insights.quote: We'll see how it how it plays out.

insights.claim: Patel says acquisition speed comes from putting the most motivated, highest-speed people on high-priority acquisition teams, since good people exist but are scattered and properly incentivized and resourced individuals drive results.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Program outcomes depend heavily on individual PMs; track leadership of key programs as a leading indicator.
insights.quote: make sure my my highest speed individuals humans are part of that acquisition team and they will they will move mountains

insights.claim: In wartime, quick reaction capabilities get on contract fast because some policies are waived and contingency operations funding supplements regular service budgets, while modular architecture concerns are deprioritized; peacetime reverts to FAR rules, competitive prototyping and source selection.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Conflict escalation sharply accelerates defense tech contracting and can entrench non-modular incumbents.

insights.claim: Patel describes navigating the Pentagon as primarily a people and organizational problem: the PM owns neither requirements, resources, contracting nor T&E, and industry has one of the biggest votes on whether a strategy succeeds.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Vendors with deep Pentagon relationships and early stakeholder engagement have structural advantage in winning programs.

insights.claim: On the TITAN program around 2022, Patel awarded four SBIR direct-to-phase-II contracts (he says he was the first to use that concept) for synthetic data, and the companies immediately asked for representative real data, which was lacking.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Synthetic data vendors in defense are gated by access to real representative data; evaluate their data-access position.
insights.quote: Hey, do you have representative data?" And I'm like, "Oh crap.

insights.claim: Military sensors can be two or three years older than commercial ones with different look angles and biomes, so commercial synthetic data advances (e.g., from Nvidia and autonomous vehicle firms) don't transfer directly to Army sensors.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Commercial AV synthetic-data leaders face a domain gap entering defense; specialized defense synthetic data has room.

insights.claim: Patel does not believe AI and autonomy can yet be built on synthetic data alone; synthetic data augments operationally relevant data and is best used to generate edge cases lacking real data.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Synthetic data is a complement, not a replacement; real-data collection remains the core spend.
insights.quote: I think synthetic data augments um uh uh operationally relevant data or actual actual data.

insights.claim: Patel says active data poisoning is happening now in open-source datasets, frameworks and databases, through deliberate bad data or accidental mislabeling, so models are already coming out biased.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Data provenance and red-teaming tools for open-source AI supply chains are a growing defense requirement.

insights.claim: Fielded computer vision can be spoofed by camouflage or graffiti on a target never seen in training, and the electromagnetic spectrum can be spoofed by something as simple as a wagon with sensors emulating a large military movement.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Counter-spoofing, robust CV and multi-sensor verification are investable capability gaps.
insights.quote: all you need is a wagon with a bunch of sensors on there that uh uh act like a a military movement

insights.claim: Patel warns against over-testing models: a model may only need to be about 80% good because the enemy, environment and operator all affect outcomes, and models must reach the field to experience real conditions.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Expect a push toward 'good enough' fielding thresholds, faster deployments and iterative updates.
insights.quote: this model needs to be 80% because um the enemy is going to have a boat, the environment is going to have a boat.

insights.claim: Patel recommends partnering with the intelligence community to catalog adversary spoofing tactics, then generating synthetic versions (e.g., graffitied targets) to inject into T&E and training datasets.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Links IC threat intel, synthetic data and T&E into a combined adversarial-robustness offering.

insights.claim: Patel cites an NDAA-directed study concluding the department must centralize on a standard for AI test and evaluation, because reliable T&E is what allows AI to scale from one-offs to large production quantities.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Standardized AI T&E is a gating item for scaled procurement; T&E tooling vendors benefit.

insights.claim: Patel says the planned next step is separating AI (data and models) from software, just as hardware was once separated from software, so models can be updated without reaccrediting the entire software package under the RMF cyber process.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: If RMF evolves to accredit model updates separately, deployment cadence for defense AI could jump sharply.

insights.claim: Patel says autonomy is not more widespread because of trust (autonomy still goes wrong more than is publicized), policy gaps on letting systems act autonomously, difficulty distinguishing combatants from civilians, and manufacturing/supply chain limits that are ramping up due to White House actions.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop and policy constraints slow fully autonomous adoption; manufacturing ramp is a tailwind for autonomy hardware makers.

insights.claim: Patel predicts that once the Pentagon's current fascination with products fades, it will realize it needs qualified integration teams, which he argues positions large integrators like Accenture Federal Services.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: A potential rotation of defense AI spend from product companies toward systems integrators; note the speaker's commercial bias.
insights.quote: right now the department is 100% fascinated by products, right? But once the the shiny toy of products is over

insights.claim: Patel says Accenture is building partnerships with OpenAI, Palantir, Anthropic and Databricks to meet government requirements rapidly, and expects significant developments in the next 2-3 months requiring heavy hiring.
insights.speaker: Bharat Patel
insights.so_what: Watch for Accenture Federal contract wins or announcements involving these AI partners in the near term.
